scenes.headline: Functions & Scope
scenes.subtitle: Reusable blocks of logic and where names live
scenes.narration: Functions package logic into reusable units, and scope decides where each variable can be seen.

scenes.headline: Why functions matter
items: Give a chunk of logic a clear name
scenes.narration: Functions let you write a piece of logic once and call it from anywhere, which keeps your pipelines from drowning in copy-pasted code. Giving that logic a descriptive name turns a wall of statements into a readable story of what the program does. Because functions take arguments and return results, they behave like predictable building blocks you can wire together. And that clear boundary makes each function far easier to test and debug in isolation.

scenes.headline: Defining and calling a function
scenes.code:
def calculate_sum(a, b):
    return a + b

result = calculate_sum(5, 7)
print(result)
scenes.narration: The def keyword defines a function that takes two parameters and returns their sum. We then call it with the arguments five and seven, and the returned value is stored in result. Printing result shows twelve, demonstrating how a function receives inputs and hands back an output.

scenes.headline: Scope lookup order (LEGB)
scenes.narration: When Python meets a name, it searches scopes in a fixed order. It first checks the local scope inside the current function, then any enclosing function, then the global module level, and finally the built-in names that ship with Python. This LEGB rule explains exactly which variable a name refers to at any point.

scenes.headline: Local versus global scope
scenes.narration: Variables created inside a function are local, meaning they exist only while the function runs and vanish when it returns. Global variables live at the module level and stay visible everywhere, but they make code harder to reason about when many functions can change them. As a rule, prefer passing data in and out through arguments and return values rather than leaning on globals.

scenes.text: Small, well-named functions with clear inputs and outputs are the backbone of maintainable code.
scenes.narration: The habit to build is keeping functions small and focused, because clear inputs and outputs are what make code easy to reuse and maintain.
